blocks.text: Every real dataset has at least one column full of raw human typed text: names, emails, addresses, product descriptions, reference codes. Numbers behave themselves. Text almost never does. Somebody typed extra spaces, somebody else used all caps, a data entry system smashed a customer code and a country abbreviation into one field. If you have already been through the filtering, removing duplicates, or renaming columns lessons in this module, you have seen the .str accessor make a brief appearance each time, always with a promise that the real depth was coming later. This is that lesson.
1. Introduction

Before you touch any individual method, you need to understand why pandas even needs something called .str in the first place. It is not decoration. Without it, most of the text cleaning you want to do simply will not run.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"customer_name": ["JOHN SMITH", "maria garcia", "David Chen"]})

df["customer_name"].lower()
# AttributeError: 'Series' object has no attribute 'lower'

blocks.text: That error is not a bug in pandas, it is pandas being precise. .lower() is a method that lives on individual Python str objects. A pandas column, a Series, is a container holding many values, not a single string. Calling a string only method directly on the container makes no more sense than calling it on a list or a dictionary. The values inside might be strings, but the Series itself is not one.

code.content:
df["customer_name"].str.lower()
# 0      john smith
# 1    maria garcia
# 2      david chen
# Name: customer_name, dtype: object

blocks.text: Adding .str in between tells pandas something specific: reach inside this Series, treat every single value as a string, run .lower() on each one individually, and hand back a new Series built from all those individual results, in the same order, with the same index. That is the whole trick.

blocks.alt: A Series where a plain lower call fails with an error while the same call through the str accessor succeeds
blocks.caption: Calling a string method directly on a Series fails. Going through .str works.

blocks.text: This should feel familiar if you have done any numeric work in pandas already. df['price'] * 1.1 does not multiply the whole column as one blob, it multiplies every single number in that column by 1.1 and returns a new Series of results. .str is the exact same idea, just for text instead of numbers. Pandas calls this vectorized behavior: one instruction, applied elementwise across every row, instead of you writing a loop yourself.

blocks.title: Quick callback
blocks.content: The filtering lesson previewed .str.contains() for text based filtering, and the renaming columns lesson used .str.lower().str.strip().str.replace() chained directly onto df.columns to clean up column names in one pass. Both of those were glimpses of exactly what you are about to learn properly here, just applied to a slightly different target, column labels instead of column values.

blocks.text: 1.1 Why a Plain Python String Method Fails

Under the hood, a pandas column made of text is usually stored with dtype object, which really just means each cell holds a reference to a regular Python object, most commonly a regular str. Pandas does not automatically know you want to run a string operation across all of them just because the values happen to be strings.

code.content:
df["customer_name"].dtype
# dtype('O')   the O stands for object

blocks.text: 1.2 The Vectorized Mental Model

Compare that object dtype to a numeric column, which gets a proper dtype like int64 or float64. Pandas knows exactly what kind of values live inside a numeric column, so arithmetic operators work directly on the whole Series without any extra accessor. Text columns do not get that same specialized treatment by default, which is exactly why .str exists: it is the bridge that tells pandas how to treat an object column full of strings as a batch of text to operate on. Once you see it that way, every method underneath it becomes predictable.

items: Start with a Series, a single text column pulled out of a DataFrame.
Add .str, which switches pandas into string mode for that Series.
Add the method you actually want, along with whatever arguments it needs.
Get back a new Series or DataFrame, same length, same order, values transformed.

blocks.text: Every method covered in the rest of this lesson follows that exact pattern. Once .str clicks conceptually, you are really just learning a list of individual methods, not a new way of thinking.
2. Case Normalization and Whitespace

The single most common text cleaning job you will do is also the simplest: making capitalization consistent and stripping out stray whitespace. Almost every messy real world text column needs this before anything else can be done to it reliably.
2.1 str.lower and str.upper

str.lower() and str.upper() normalize case across an entire Series in one call. This matters more than it sounds like it should, because two values that look identical to a human, Corp and CORP, are two completely different strings as far as Python is concerned. Comparisons, groupbys, and merges all fail silently when case is inconsistent, they just quietly treat matching values as different groups.

code.content:
df["status"] = pd.Series(["Active", "ACTIVE", "active", "Inactive"])
df["status"].str.lower()
# 0      active
# 1      active
# 2      active
# 3    inactive
# dtype: object

blocks.text: 2.2 str.strip for Leading and Trailing Whitespace

str.strip() removes whitespace from the start and end of every value, the kind of stray space or tab that sneaks in from copy pasted data, CSV exports, or manual data entry. str.lstrip() and str.rstrip() exist too, for when you only want to trim one side.

code.content:
df["city"] = pd.Series(["  Mumbai", "Delhi   ", " Bengaluru "])
df["city"].str.strip()
# 0       Mumbai
# 1        Delhi
# 2    Bengaluru
# dtype: object

blocks.alt: A messy string with mixed case and extra spaces passing through strip then lower to become clean
blocks.caption: Chaining strip and lower turns messy raw text into a normalized value.

blocks.title: strip only touches the edges
blocks.content: str.strip() will not fix double spaces sitting inside a value, like John and Smith separated by three spaces instead of one. That is an internal problem, not a leading or trailing one, and it needs str.replace with a regex pattern instead, which is exactly where the next section goes.

blocks.text: 3. Substituting Text with str.replace
str.replace() swaps out pieces of text across an entire Series. It comes in two flavors depending on one parameter, regex, and picking the right one matters for both correctness and speed.
3.1 Literal Substring Replacement
With regex set to False, str.replace() looks for an exact literal piece of text and swaps it out wherever it appears, character for character, no pattern matching involved.

code.content:
df["price_text"] = pd.Series(["$1,200", "$450", "$3,000"])
df["price_text"].str.replace("$", "", regex=False)
# 0    1,200
# 1      450
# 2    3,000
# dtype: object

blocks.text: Literal mode is the right default whenever the thing you are replacing is a fixed, known piece of text, a currency symbol, a specific word, a known typo. It is also slightly faster than regex mode, since pandas does not need to compile and evaluate a pattern for every value.
3.2 Pattern Based Replacement with Regex

With regex set to True, the first argument to str.replace() is treated as a regular expression pattern instead of a literal string, so it can match a whole family of text rather than one exact sequence.

code.content:
df["notes"] = pd.Series(["too   many    spaces", "just one gap", "no  extra   here"])
df["notes"].str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True)
# 0    too many spaces
# 1        just one gap
# 2       no extra here
# dtype: object

blocks.text: That pattern, backslash s plus, matches one or more whitespace characters in a row and collapses each run down to a single space. A literal replacement could never do that, because there is no one fixed string to search for, just a repeating pattern.

blocks.alt: A text column branching into literal replace swapping exact text and regex replace swapping every pattern match
blocks.caption: Literal replace swaps one exact string. Regex replace swaps every match of a pattern.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Parameter","What it matches","Typical use case"],"rows":[["regex=False","One exact literal string","Removing a known symbol or fixed word"],["regex=True","Any text matching a pattern","Collapsing whitespace, stripping digits, matching varied formats"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Splitting Strings into Parts

Sometimes a single column is secretly carrying two or three pieces of information at once, a full name that should be a first and last name, a location string that should be a city and a state. str.split() is how you tear those apart.
4.1 str.split Basics
str.split() breaks each value on a delimiter you specify and returns a Series where every entry is a Python list of the pieces.

code.content:
df["location"] = pd.Series(["Chennai, TN", "Pune, MH", "Kochi, KL"])
df["location"].str.split(", ")
# 0    [Chennai, TN]
# 1       [Pune, MH]
# 2      [Kochi, KL]
# dtype: object

blocks.text: That is useful on its own if you just need the pieces available for further processing, but a Series full of lists is awkward to work with directly. Most of the time what you actually want is real separate columns, which is exactly what the expand parameter gives you.

blocks.alt: An address string being split on a comma into a Series of list values
blocks.caption: str.split breaks each value into a list of pieces on the delimiter you give it.

blocks.text: 4.2 expand=True: Turning a Split Into New Columns
Pass expand=True and str.split() stops returning a Series of lists and instead returns a full DataFrame, one column per split piece, aligned by position.

code.content:
df[["city", "state"]] = df["location"].str.split(", ", expand=True)
df[["city", "state"]]
#       city state
# 0  Chennai    TN
# 1     Pune    MH
# 2    Kochi    KL

blocks.alt: A Series of list values expanding into two separate new columns side by side
blocks.caption: expand=True turns the split result directly into real columns instead of a column of lists.

blocks.title: Watch the piece count
blocks.content: expand=True assumes every row splits into the same number of pieces. If one row has an extra comma somewhere and produces three pieces while the rest produce two, pandas fills the missing spot with NaN rather than erroring, which can quietly break a column assignment if you are not checking for it. Passing n=1 to limit the split to a fixed number of cuts is a common way to keep the piece count predictable.

blocks.text: 5. Extracting Text with a Regex Capture Group

str.split() works well when a value is cleanly separated by a delimiter. Plenty of real data is not that polite. A numeric ID might be buried in the middle of a longer string with no consistent delimiter around it at all. That is what str.extract() is for.
5.1 str.extract Fundamentals

str.extract() takes a regular expression with one or more capture groups, the parts of the pattern wrapped in parentheses, and returns a DataFrame with one column per capture group, holding whatever matched inside those parentheses.

code.content:
df["ticket"] = pd.Series(["TICKET-4521-OPEN", "TICKET-9087-CLOSED", "TICKET-1130-OPEN"])
df["ticket"].str.extract(r"TICKET-(\d+)-")
#       0
# 0  4521
# 1  9087
# 2  1130

blocks.alt: Mixed text with an embedded number being pulled out by a regex capture group into its own Series
blocks.caption: str.extract pulls just the piece matched by the capture group, leaving the rest behind.

blocks.text: 5.2 Extracting a Numeric ID from Mixed Text
Name the column while you are at it by using a named group, so the result comes back with a real column label instead of the default 0.

code.content:
df["ticket_id"] = df["ticket"].str.extract(r"TICKET-(?P<ticket_id>\d+)-")
df[["ticket", "ticket_id"]]
#                 ticket ticket_id
#  0   TICKET-4521-OPEN       4521
#  1 TICKET-9087-CLOSED       9087
#  2   TICKET-1130-OPEN       1130

blocks.title: No match means NaN, not an error
blocks.content: If a row does not match the pattern at all, str.extract() puts NaN in that row rather than raising an exception. This is the same passthrough philosophy the whole str family follows, a mismatch is treated as missing data, not a crash, which means one badly formatted row will not stop your entire pipeline.

blocks.text: 6. Checking String Content

Sometimes you do not need to transform text at all, you just need a yes or no answer about what is inside it, is this word present, does this value start a certain way. These checks return a boolean Series, which makes them a natural fit for filtering, something the filtering lesson touched on already with a single example.
6.1 str.contains for Substring and Pattern Matching
str.contains() checks whether each value contains a given substring or matches a given pattern anywhere inside it, and returns True or False for every row.

code.content:
df["email"] = pd.Series(["a@gmail.com", "b@yahoo.com", "c@gmail.com"])
df["email"].str.contains("gmail")
# 0     True
# 1    False
# 2     True
# dtype: bool

blocks.text: By default str.contains() treats the pattern as a regex, so characters like a dot carry their special regex meaning unless you pass regex=False. It also takes a case parameter for case insensitive matching, and an na parameter that controls what value gets used for rows where the underlying text is missing, since a plain True or False cannot describe an unknown.
6.2 str.startswith and str.endswith

str.contains() matches anywhere in the string. str.startswith() and str.endswith() are stricter, anchored checks, they only return True if the match sits right at the beginning or right at the end of the value.

code.content:
df["sku"] = pd.Series(["ELEC-4521", "FURN-1123", "ELEC-9087"])
df["sku"].str.startswith("ELEC")
# 0     True
# 1    False
# 2     True
# dtype: bool

df["sku"].str.endswith("87")
# 0    False
# 1    False
# 2     True
# dtype: bool

blocks.alt: A text column checked three ways, contains anywhere, startswith at the front, endswith at the back
blocks.caption: Three related checks on the same column: anywhere, only the start, or only the end.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Method","Where it checks","Example use"],"rows":[["str.contains","Anywhere in the string","Finding rows that mention a keyword"],["str.startswith","Only the beginning of the string","Filtering by a category prefix like a SKU code"],["str.endswith","Only the end of the string","Filtering by a file extension or suffix code"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Measuring String Length with str.len

str.len() returns the character count of every value in a Series as an integer. On its own it sounds almost too simple to matter, but it is one of the fastest data quality checks you can run on a text column.

code.content:
df["comment"] = pd.Series(["ok", "This looks great, thanks for the fast delivery", "n/a"])
df["comment"].str.len()
# 0     2
# 1    48
# 2     3
# dtype: int64

df[df["comment"].str.len() < 5]
#   comment
# 0      ok
# 2     n/a

blocks.text: A cluster of suspiciously short entries often means placeholder text, blank submissions, or a data entry shortcut like typing na instead of leaving a field empty. A cluster of suspiciously long entries can mean the wrong field got pasted into the wrong column entirely. Either way, str.len() combined with a simple filter surfaces both problems in one line.

blocks.alt: A text column measured by length and bucketed into suspiciously short, normal, and suspiciously long entries
blocks.caption: str.len turns character count into a quick data quality signal.

blocks.title: Length on missing values
blocks.content: str.len() follows the same rule as every other str method: a NaN entry in the column produces NaN as its length rather than 0 or an error. If you are filtering on length and want to also catch missing values in the same pass, you need to handle NaN explicitly rather than assuming it behaves like an empty string.

blocks.text: 8. Concatenating String Columns
Combining two or more text columns into one is common enough to deserve its own section: building a full address out of street, city, and postal code, or a display name out of first and last name.
8.1 Using the Plus Operator
String Series support the plus operator directly, joining values from two columns position by position, exactly like arithmetic addition does for numbers.

code.content:
df["first"] = pd.Series(["Anita", "Rohan"])
df["last"] = pd.Series(["Rao", "Verma"])
df["full_name"] = df["first"] + " " + df["last"]
df["full_name"]
# 0      Anita Rao
# 1    Rohan Verma
# dtype: object

blocks.text: Notice the plain space sitting between the two columns being added, plus does not insert a separator for you automatically, you have to supply one yourself as its own literal piece of the expression.
8.2 str.cat for More Control

str.cat() does the same job as chained plus operators but in a single call, with a sep parameter for the separator and an na_rep parameter that controls what gets substituted in for any missing values instead of letting them wipe out the whole combined result.

code.content:
df["full_name"] = df["first"].str.cat(df["last"], sep=" ", na_rep="unknown")
df["full_name"]
# 0      Anita Rao
# 1    Rohan Verma
# dtype: object

blocks.text: For two columns, plus and str.cat land in roughly the same place. str.cat() starts to pay off once you are combining three or more columns at once, or when you specifically need control over how missing values get handled during the join, something plus cannot do for you at all.

blocks.alt: First and last name columns joining through either the plus operator or str.cat into one combined full name column
blocks.caption: Both the plus operator and str.cat join columns together, str.cat just adds more control.

blocks.text: 9. Missing Values in String Columns

String columns get missing values just like numeric ones do, and every method covered so far in this lesson has been quietly following one consistent rule around them, worth calling out explicitly now.
9.1 How NaN Passes Through str Methods

When a value in a string Series is NaN, running a str method on that Series does not error out on the missing row and does not skip it either. It simply carries the NaN forward untouched, right through the same operation being applied to every other, real, value.

code.content:
df["name"] = pd.Series(["Priya", None, "Arjun"])
df["name"].str.upper()
# 0    PRIYA
# 1      NaN
# 2    ARJUN
# dtype: object

blocks.alt: A NaN value passing through a str method untouched while a real string value gets transformed normally
blocks.caption: NaN rides through a str method unchanged instead of causing an error.

blocks.text: This is deliberate design, not a loophole. A raw Python float, which is what a missing value in an object column technically is under the hood, genuinely has no upper method, so calling it directly the plain Python way really would throw an error. The str accessor is specifically built to check for missing values first and route around them automatically, so one gap in your data does not take down the entire column operation.

blocks.title: Why this matters in practice
blocks.content: Because NaN quietly survives every str call, you can chain several str methods together, strip, then lower, then replace, without adding manual checks in between for missing rows. The gap just rides along to the end unchanged. It only becomes something you need to actively handle once you are ready to fill it in or filter it out.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example: Cleaning Messy Customer Names

Time to put the whole toolkit together on something that looks like it came straight out of a real production database: a customer_name column with inconsistent capitalization and stray whitespace, sitting next to a customer_ref column that has a numeric customer code buried inside a longer reference string.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_name": ["  JOHN SMITH", "maria garcia ", "David   Chen", " Sarah O'Connor", "MICHAEL brown  "],
    "customer_ref": ["REF-00482-US", "ref-01133-us", "REF-00219-CA", "Ref-00875-US", "REF-01560-CA"],
})
df["customer_name"].tolist()
# ['  JOHN SMITH', 'maria garcia ', 'David   Chen', " Sarah O'Connor", 'MICHAEL brown  ']

blocks.text: 10.1 Normalizing Case and Whitespace First

Before splitting anything, the whitespace and casing need to be predictable, otherwise the split step downstream will produce inconsistent results. This chains three methods from earlier sections in one line: strip to remove the leading and trailing spaces, a regex replace to collapse any internal double spaces down to one, and title to make the capitalization consistent.

code.content:
df["customer_name"] = (
    df["customer_name"]
    .str.strip()
    .str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True)
    .str.title()
)
df["customer_name"]
# 0        John Smith
# 1      Maria Garcia
# 2        David Chen
# 3    Sarah O'Connor
# 4     Michael Brown
# Name: customer_name, dtype: object

blocks.text: Every value is now a single space separated pair of words with matching capitalization, which is exactly the predictable shape str.split() needs to work reliably in the next step.
10.2 Splitting into first_name and last_name with expand=True
With the text normalized, splitting on the single remaining space and expanding the result straight into two new columns is a one liner.

code.content:
df[["first_name", "last_name"]] = df["customer_name"].str.split(" ", n=1, expand=True)
df[["first_name", "last_name"]]
#   first_name  last_name
# 0       John      Smith
# 1      Maria     Garcia
# 2      David       Chen
# 3      Sarah   O'Connor
# 4    Michael      Brown

blocks.alt: A messy full name column being cleaned with strip and replace then split with expand true into first_name and last_name columns
blocks.caption: The full pipeline: normalize the text first, then split it straight into two real columns.

blocks.title: Why n=1 is doing real work here
blocks.content: n=1 caps the split at a single cut, so anything after the first space, including a name that would otherwise have three or four words in it, lands entirely in last_name instead of overflowing into extra columns. Without it, a three word name would produce a third column full of NaN for every other row, exactly the piece count mismatch problem flagged back in the split section.

blocks.text: 10.3 Extracting a Numeric Customer Code from a Reference String

The customer_ref column mixes inconsistent casing on the prefix with a numeric code and a country suffix, all glued together with no clean delimiter to split on cleanly. This is precisely the situation str.extract() exists for.

code.content:
df["customer_code"] = df["customer_ref"].str.extract(r"(?i)ref-(\d+)-")
df[["customer_ref", "customer_code"]]
#    customer_ref customer_code
# 0  REF-00482-US         00482
# 1  ref-01133-us         01133
# 2  REF-00219-CA         00219
# 3  Ref-00875-US         00875
# 4  REF-01560-CA         01560

blocks.text: The (?i) flag at the start of the pattern makes the match case insensitive, so REF, ref, and Ref all match the same way despite the inconsistent casing seen across this column. The capture group around the digits pulls out exactly the numeric code and nothing else, leaving the case noise and the country suffix behind entirely.
11. Recap: The str Accessor Toolkit

Every method in this lesson follows the same pattern established at the very start: a Series, dot str, dot the method you need. Once that clicks, the rest is really just building a mental catalog of what is available.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Method","What it does"],"rows":[["str.lower / str.upper","Normalize case across every value"],["str.strip","Remove leading and trailing whitespace"],["str.replace","Substitute text, literal or regex pattern"],["str.split","Break each value into parts on a delimiter"],["str.split with expand=True","Turn split parts into real columns"],["str.extract","Pull text matching a regex capture group"],["str.contains","Check for a substring or pattern anywhere"],["str.startswith / str.endswith","Anchored checks at the start or end"],["str.len","Count characters, useful for quality checks"],["+ or str.cat","Join string columns together"]]}

blocks.text: Text data will keep showing up messy no matter how careful the upstream systems are. The good news is that every one of these methods handles missing values the same predictable way, passes them through untouched, so you can chain several together with confidence and clean up the real problems one method at a time.
